turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: One hundred and forty-nine, you say? A rather large number, wouldn't you agree? It suggests a certain… expansiveness, which is not always a desirable quality in a gentleman, particularly when one is attempting to cultivate an air of refined restraint.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I… I hadn't considered it in that light, Lady Bracknell. Belgrave Square is quite extensive, you see, and numbers tend to run rather high. Perhaps it simply reflects the size of the family’s holdings?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Holdings, Mr. Worthing? A convenient explanation, though scarcely convincing. One does not simply *acquire* such expansive properties without a certain… pedigree, wouldn't you concur? Let us move on, then, to more pertinent matters.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. My family, while not possessing a title, has… has always been respectable, I assure you. I believe my father—my *adopted* father—was a man of considerable standing in his community.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Respectable, you say? Respectability is a most agreeable quality, Mr. Worthing, but it is, alas, far too easily assumed. It requires, you understand, a foundation—a lineage, if you will—and I confess I detect a distinct lack of demonstrable roots in your narrative thus far. Pray, enlighten me further about this 'adopted' father; his profession, at the very least, would be a starting point.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mother, must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so relentlessly? He is perfectly satisfactory, and I have already declared my intentions, as you know. It’s dreadfully awkward for everyone involved, especially Mr. Worthing, to have him subjected to such a… *thorough* examination.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Awkwardness, Miss Fairfax, is a most unfortunate consequence of precipitate declarations. Your sentiments, however charming, cannot override the imperative of establishing a gentleman’s suitability. Now, Mr. Worthing, let us return to this ‘adopted’ father—a most curious circumstance, indeed—and you will endeavor to provide me with a name and occupation, if you please.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! You’re being absolutely dreadful. Mr. Worthing is quite capable of explaining himself, and I’m sure he finds your grilling rather… unsettling, don’t you, Mr. Worthing?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My… my adopted father, Lady Bracknell, was… a General. Yes, a General! A man of great military distinction, I’m told, though I, regrettably, never knew him personally. It’s all rather… hazy, you see.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A General! How very… convenient. While military service certainly implies a certain degree of discipline, it does not, I regret to say, automatically confer respectability. We must, Mr. Worthing, delve deeper into the particulars of this General; his lineage, his affiliations, and, above all, his social standing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. His name, I believe, was Sir Archibald, though the precise title… well, family lore is rather unreliable, I’m afraid. I’m happy to endeavor to recall more, if it would be of assistance.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Sir Archibald! The name possesses a certain… resonance. However, resonance, Mr. Worthing, is a poor substitute for documented heritage. We shall, I fear, require considerably more information before I can even *consider* allowing my daughter to be associated with a gentleman whose paternal history is shrouded in such nebulous uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A hazy recollection, you say, Lady Bracknell? I assure you, I strive to be as forthcoming as possible; it’s simply that these details... they weren't precisely *communicated* to me, being, as you know, found. I do possess a silver hand mirror, though—a rather handsome one—perhaps that could serve as some kind of… heirloom?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A silver hand mirror! Really, Mr. Worthing, you offer me a *mirror* as evidence of ancestral connection? One might as well present a looking-glass and expect it to reveal the secrets of the aristocracy! It is a most peculiar proposition, and frankly, rather unsettling.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Oh, dear, a looking-glass, you say? I… I hadn't quite intended to imply a direct lineage, Lady Bracknell. It was merely… a token, a small object of personal value, you see. Perhaps I should have chosen something different?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A token! Mr. Worthing, you appear to believe that sentimentality can compensate for a lack of lineage. It cannot. Indeed, the very notion is almost… vulgar. Let us proceed, shall we? I believe I asked about your profession?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My profession, Lady Bracknell? Well, I'm a… a guardian, of sorts. I look after a young ward, Miss Cecily Cardew, and I endeavour to provide for her and guide her moral development – a responsibility I take very seriously, you understand.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A guardian, you say? It appears you have taken upon yourself a duty, Mr. Worthing, which is commendable, though hardly a substitute for a respectable income and a suitable family background. Tell me, this Miss Cardew… is she amenable to your influence, or does she possess a rebellious spirit that might, heaven forbid, infect my own daughter?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so relentlessly? He is perfectly suitable, and I’ve already made my intentions quite clear. One would think you’d be delighted!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Delighted, my dear? Your enthusiasm is… touching, but premature. One does not declare an engagement lightly, Gwendolen, especially when the gentleman in question is being subjected to a rather thorough assessment, wouldn't you agree, Mr. Worthing?

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
